analysis.investment_thesis: Exim Routes shows eye-catching 134% revenue CAGR and stellar ROE/ROCE numbers, but it is a commodity paper-recycling intermediary with zero free cash flow, a P/E of 37.5x, and only 6 years of operating history — failing three of my core SMILE criteria. The growth is real, but the business model has no moat and the market is pricing it as if it does.
key_strengths: Explosive revenue growth — ₹4 Cr to ₹121 Cr in 4 years (134% CAGR) with margins expanding (EBITDA margin ~8.3% in FY25)
High capital efficiency on a thin equity base — ROE 54%, ROCE 55% — shows strong asset-light trading economics
Debt-to-equity ~0.36 (₹9 Cr borrowings / ₹25 Cr equity) — not over-leveraged yet
key_risks: Negative OCF all 5 years with FCF at -₹9 Cr in FY25 — profit exists on paper but cash is being consumed, classic working capital trap in commodity trading
P/E of 37.5x on ₹8 Cr net profit is 2-4x my preferred small-cap entry range (8-15x) for a commoditised, low-moat business
Company incorporated April 2019 — only 6 years old with no experience through a credit or commodity cycle, far below my 'medium experience' threshold
red_flags: OCF negative in 0/5 years — business has never generated positive operating cash flow
Financing CF positive every year — company is consistently raising external capital just to fund operations
Commodity trading intermediary has no durable moat; replicable by any well-funded competitor
Total assets tripled in one year (₹21 Cr → ₹54 Cr) while cash burn accelerated — receivables/payables mismatch growing dangerously
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Exim Routes is a recyclable paper trading platform connecting global suppliers to Indian paper mills. The revenue hockey stick (₹4 Cr → ₹121 Cr) is impressive, but the business is a commodity intermediary — it buys and sells paper waste with thin ~8% EBITDA margins and no pricing power. The spectacular ROE/ROCE figures (54%/55%) are an artefact of a very small equity base, not evidence of a genuine economic moat. The P/E of 37.5x is being applied to a business that any trader with working capital can replicate, which is a recipe for multiple compression.

The free cash flow story is damning for a Kedia-style investment. Despite booking ₹8 Cr of net profit in FY25, operating cash flow was -₹5 Cr and FCF was -₹9 Cr — meaning the company has never actually generated cash from operations in its entire 5-year life. Total assets tripled from ₹21 Cr to ₹54 Cr in one year while financing cash flows turned strongly positive (₹11 Cr raised) — the business is funded by external capital, not its own earnings. This is a working capital trap dressed in high growth numbers. Until the company demonstrates sustained positive FCF, a management track record through a downturn, and a valuation that reflects its commodity nature (ideally sub-15x P/E), I would stay away entirely.
